9 Materials That Help With Self-Scratching
She scratched her arms again last night — in the waiting room, just sitting there quietly, and suddenly her skin was red and raw before you could reach her. You said her name softly. She looked down at her arms like her hands had been moving on their own.
You are not failing. Your child's nervous system is speaking — in the only language it currently knows. These materials teach it a safer vocabulary.

This Is More Common Than You Know
You are among millions of families navigating this exact challenge — watching your child scratch until they bleed, feeling helpless when they can't stop even when they want to. The isolation you feel? It is not the reality.
Self-scratching is not a parenting failure. It is a nervous system seeking input, regulation, or relief — through the most available tool: the child's own skin. Your job is to give the nervous system better tools.

This Is a Wiring Difference. Not a Behavior Problem.
The Sensory Pathway
When your child scratches, the somatosensory cortex — the brain's touch-processing center — receives intense proprioceptive and tactile input. For children with sensory processing differences, this input is not "too much" — it is exactly what a dysregulated nervous system is seeking.
The Emotional Circuit
The amygdala governs threat detection and emotional flooding. When your child is anxious, overwhelmed, or overstimulated, scratching — with its intense, predictable sensation — can momentarily interrupt this flooding. It is self-generated regulation. Imperfect, damaging, but functional from the nervous system's point of view.
The Habit Loop
Over time, scratching becomes encoded in the basal ganglia as a habit loop: Trigger (anxiety/boredom/overwhelm) → Routine (scratch) → Reward (relief/sensation). The loop runs automatically, bypassing conscious decision-making. This is why your child often doesn't "know" they're doing it.
The Intervention Logic
Effective intervention doesn't fight the nervous system — it offers it superior alternatives. Textured tools replace the somatosensory input. Deep pressure interrupts the amygdala cascade. Fidgets redirect the basal ganglia habit loop. Understanding this is the foundation for everything on this page.
Sources: Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2020) | PRISMA Systematic Review (2024) | Sensory Integration Theory — Dr. A. Jean Ayres
Your Child Is Here. Here Is Where We're Heading.
Self-scratching most commonly emerges between ages 2–4, when nervous system regulation demands exceed the child's coping toolkit. Understanding where your child sits on the developmental timeline helps you choose the right approach — and set realistic expectations.
Ages 0–2
Sensory system calibrating. Mouthing, touching, grabbing — normal tactile exploration. Early sensory preferences emerge.
Ages 2–4 ⚠️ Current Zone
Self-scratching most commonly emerges here. Nervous system regulation demands exceed coping toolkit. BFRB patterns begin to form.
Ages 4–7 🔵 Intervention Window
Neural plasticity at its peak. Best window for establishing alternative sensory strategies. Habit loops not yet fully entrenched.
Ages 7–10
Habit loops more established but still modifiable. Awareness-based approaches add effectiveness. School context adds social dimension.
Ages 10–12+
Emotional regulation layer becomes primary. Adolescent identity intersects with BFRB stigma. Peer support adds importance.

Common Co-occurring Conditions: Autism Spectrum (ASD) · ADHD · Anxiety Disorders · OCD Spectrum · Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD). Presence of co-occurring conditions does NOT reduce intervention effectiveness — it shapes which materials work best.

The Technique: What It Is
Multi-Modal BFRB Redirection
Sensory Substitution Protocol
Parent-Friendly Alias: "Materials That Meet the Need Safely"
Self-scratching is a Body-Focused Repetitive Behavior (BFRB) in which a child repetitively scratches their own skin, causing redness, wounds, scarring, or infection. It exists on a spectrum from sensory-seeking habit to diagnosable excoriation disorder.
This intervention introduces 9 categories of therapeutic materials that provide equivalent or superior sensory input without tissue damage, occupy hands to interrupt automatic scratching patterns, create physical barriers while urges are being managed, and support nervous system regulation at the root level.
The goal is NOT to suppress the behavior — it is to meet the underlying need through safer channels until the child's nervous system develops broader regulation capacity.
🏷️ Domain
Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviors (BFRB) / Self-Scratching / Tactile Seeking
🏷️ Age Range
2–12 years
🏷️ Duration
Materials all-day available. Active protocol: 5–15 min.
🏷️ Setting
Home • School • Community • All environments
This Technique Lives Across Five Disciplines
Self-scratching doesn't respect clinical boundaries — and effective intervention doesn't either. The Pinnacle FusionModule™ coordinates all four disciplines so the child receives one integrated plan, not four competing ones.
Occupational Therapy (OT) — Primary Lead
Leads sensory assessment, designs the sensory diet, selects textured and proprioceptive materials, teaches parents to read sensory profiles, and trains sensory substitution protocols. OT owns the sensory domain.
Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA/BCBA)
Conducts functional behavior assessment (FBA) to identify scratching triggers and functions. Designs differential reinforcement programs, builds competing behaviors, and tracks frequency and intensity data.
NeuroDevelopmental Pediatrics
Rules out dermatological causes, assesses for OCD spectrum, anxiety, or excoriation disorder diagnosis, coordinates medication review when relevant, and monitors skin health and infection.
SLP + Special Education
SLP builds emotional vocabulary so the child can identify and communicate the urge. SpEd designs school-based accommodation plans and coordinates with teachers on sensory tool access.
Precision Intervention. Not Random Activity.
Every material on this page targets a specific, observable outcome. Understanding the layered targets helps you choose the right tool for the right moment — and measure real progress.
🎯 Primary Target
Sensory Input Redirection — Child reaches for tool instead of skin
🎯 Secondary Targets
Behavior Interruption · Emotional Regulation · Skin Protection — Child notices urge, uses alternate strategy, wounds heal
🎯 Developmental Gains
Interoception · Self-Advocacy · Parental Confidence — Child communicates needs; parent has a concrete toolkit
9 Materials. One for Every Function Scratching Serves.
Backed by Canon Taxonomy
Sourced to Indian Market
Each material below maps to a specific function scratching serves. Matching material to function is the key to success. A smooth toy will not replace an intense scratching sensation — always match the intensity of the need.
Textured Sensory Tools
Spiky sensory balls, silicone brushes, textured fidget rings, velcro strips. ₹150–800. The urge seeks INTENSITY — match it.
Fidget Tools & Hand Occupiers
Tangle toys, therapy putty, fidget cubes, marble-in-mesh fidgets. ₹100–600. Must fully occupy BOTH hands.
Compression Clothing & Skin Barriers
Compression arm sleeves, full-length shirts, leggings, sensory vests. ₹500–2,000. Creates barrier AND provides calming proprioceptive input.
Cold / Temperature-Based Tools
Reusable gel cold packs, metal sensory tools, frozen sensory toys. ₹100–500. Intense sensation with zero tissue damage.
Skin Protection & Healing Support
Protective sleeves, liquid bandage, healing ointment, moisturizing lotion, nail file, cotton gloves. ₹200–1,000. Harm reduction while behavioral change builds.
Deep Pressure & Proprioceptive Tools
Weighted blanket (max 10% body weight), weighted lap pad, body sock, compression vest. ₹800–3,500. Maximum calming proprioceptive input.
Emotional Regulation & Coping Tools
Emotion identification cards, coping strategy cards, calm-down kit, Hoberman sphere, feelings thermometer. ₹200–1,200. Practice during CALM times only.
Awareness & Habit-Interruption Tools
Silicone awareness bracelets, beaded bracelets, habit tracking charts, mindfulness cards, textured rings. ₹100–500. Must NEVER create shame — only noticing.
Sensory Diet & Proactive Regulation Tools
Sensory diet schedules, kinetic sand, play dough, movement break timers, transition sensory kit. ₹0–1,000. Prevention beats intervention.

Read This Before Introducing Any Material
Clinical precision. Parental empathy. Your child's safety is the absolute baseline. Review all three zones before beginning.
🔴 RED ZONE — STOP. Do Not Proceed If:
• Scratching has caused wounds requiring medical attention — address medical care FIRST. • Signs of skin infection: warmth, swelling, discharge, fever. Seek medical care immediately. • Scratching appears intentional self-harm — requires mental health professional involvement first. • Child is in acute distress or meltdown state. Stabilize first. • Child shows extreme distress when materials are introduced. Never force any sensory tool.
⚠️ AMBER ZONE — Proceed With Caution:
• Weighted items: Maximum 10% of child's body weight. Check circulation. • Cold tools: Do not apply ice directly to skin for more than 5 minutes. Wrap in cloth. • Textured tools: Test intensity — strong enough to satisfy, not so abrasive it creates new irritation. • Compression: Should feel snug/calming, not restrictive. Child must be able to remove independently. • Small fidget parts: Age-appropriate only. No small parts for children under 3 or with mouthing behaviors. • Awareness tools: Must never create shame or increase anxiety.
✅ GREEN ZONE — Go Indicators:
• Child is in a baseline calm or slightly elevated (not dysregulated) state • Wounds are healed or bandaged and medically monitored • Child has been introduced to at least one material during calm practice • Parent has read and understood the material's safety notes • Session happens in a familiar, low-demand environment

🛑STOP if you see: Child becomes more agitated with the material · Child shows signs of pain they cannot communicate · Scratching intensity immediately increases · Any sign of allergic reaction to material. 📞 If scratching has caused a wound requiring medical care, contact your pediatrician and call Pinnacle: 9100 181 181
The Right Environment Prevents 80% of Session Problems.
Room Setup Checklist
  1. Choose a room with minimal visual clutter
  1. Set lighting to warm/dimmed — not fluorescent
  1. Temperature: comfortable, not overheated
  1. Sound: quiet or low white noise — no TV, no music with lyrics
  1. Remove items that typically trigger scratching
  1. Place 2–3 alternative materials within child's arm's reach BEFORE session — not during
  1. Have reward system visible but not distracting
  1. Tell siblings/household members: quiet time
  1. Parent: phone on silent. Presence is the intervention.
  1. Water/snack available — hydrated, fed child = regulated child
Materials Placement Guide
Right Side (dominant hand)
Textured tools — first line of redirection
Left Side (non-dominant hand)
Fidget — engages both hands simultaneously
Nearby/Retrievable
Cold pack in cooler. Weighted blanket draped nearby, not on child yet.

Is Your Child Ready? The 60-Second Readiness Check
The best session is one that starts right. Run through this checklist before introducing any materials. A session abandoned at the right moment is better than a session forced through at the wrong one.
Child has eaten in the last 2 hours
Hydrated and fed = regulated nervous system baseline
Child had adequate sleep last night
Sleep deprivation significantly increases dysregulation risk
Not currently scratching at high intensity
Moderate or lower state — not acute crisis
In a familiar, safe environment
No new locations, new people, or high-demand contexts
No major stressors in last 30 minutes
Transitions, conflicts, or demands lower readiness
Parent/caregiver is calm and present
Not rushing, not distracted — your regulated presence is the intervention
ALL ✅ → GREEN LIGHT
Proceed to full protocol. Cards 14–19.
3–5 ✅ → AMBER: MODIFY
One material only. 5-minute session. No expectations — just exposure. Heavy reinforcement.
1–2 ✅ → RED: POSTPONE
Today is a data point, not a failure. Comfort, preferred activity, physical safety. Reschedule tomorrow.
Step 1 of 6
⏱️ 30–60 seconds
Begin With an Invitation, Never a Command.
Principle: ABA Pairing + OT "Just-Right Challenge" = low-demand entry. The way you offer the material is as important as the material itself.
The Exact Script
"Hey [child's name] — I found something really interesting. Want to feel this?" [Hold out the textured tool — at child's eye level, your hand open, no expectation on your face]
Alternative Scripts
🟢Sensory-seeking child: "Look what I have — it feels SO cool." 😰Anxious child: "We're just going to look at it first. You don't have to touch it yet." 🤫Non-verbal/low language: Show the object. Smile. Wait. 🧒Older child (8+): "I got something for when you feel like scratching. Want to try it?"
Body Language Guidance
  • Get to child's eye level — crouch/sit, not tower
  • Face relaxed, warm — not anxious or evaluative
  • Open body posture — no crossed arms
  • Object in open palm, not thrust toward child
  • Eye contact: offered, not demanded
Acceptance Cues ✅
Child looks at the object (even briefly) · Reaches toward it · Body relaxes slightly · Any sign of curiosity, even subtle
Resistance Cues ⚠️
Child turns away → Reduce demand: "Just sitting here with it." Child pushes object away → Accept it. Try again tomorrow. Child becomes more agitated → Stop. Offer comfort. Reschedule.
Step 2 of 6
⏱️ 1–3 minutes
The Child Is Curious. Now Deepen the Interaction.
How to Present the Material
Speed: Slow and deliberate
Never rushed or hurried — the child sets the pace
Modeling: You use it first
"Look, I like this feeling." — zero expectation at this stage
Distance: Within reach
Child initiates touch, not you
"Let's try this together. Like this — [demonstrate on your own hand first]. Now you try."
Child Response Spectrum
🟢Engagement: Child actively explores material — go deeper 🟡Tolerance: Child allows it without clear enjoyment — maintain, don't push 🔴Avoidance: Child pulls away or ignores — reduce demand, try different material
For Children with Active Scratching Urge
  1. Don't stop them verbally
  1. Silently place the textured tool next to their scratching hand
  1. Wait. Let the proximity work.
  1. If they pick it up: reinforce immediately
  1. If they don't: "This might feel even better than that."
Reinforcement Cue
When child touches the material: "You tried it! That was great!" — within 3 seconds. Specific. Warm. Not excessive.
Step 3 of 6
⏱️ 5–10 minutes
The Active Ingredient. This Is Where the Nervous System Begins to Learn a New Language.
🖐️ Textured Tool (Sensory-Seeking)
Child runs fingers across textured surface with varying pressure. "Try scratching THIS. As hard as you need." Goal: Complete sensory satiation. Let the urge be met fully — by the tool. Duration until child naturally stops or reduces intensity. Success: Child's body visibly relaxes.
🧩 Fidget (Automatic/Boredom)
Both hands engaged with fidget simultaneously. Parent narrates without demanding: "Twist it this way..." Goal: Hands fully occupied throughout high-risk activity. Success: Session ends with zero scratching episodes.
💪 Compression + Deep Pressure (Dysregulation)
Compression sleeve on. Add firm, sustained pressure to upper arms (10–15 seconds) with permission. "Squeeze time — ready?" Goal: Nervous system regulation through proprioceptive input. Success: Child visibly calms; scratching urge reduces.
🧊 Cold Tool (Intense Sensation/Anxiety)
Child holds cold pack or runs hands under cold water. "Feel that? That's intense — just like scratching, but your skin stays safe." Goal: Intense sensation provided, scratching urge temporarily satisfied. Success: Child reaches for cold tool when urge rises.

❌Common Errors: Stopping scratching BEFORE offering alternative · Using texture too light for the child's sensory threshold · Watching expectantly instead of joining · Using tools only when scratching is already happening (use proactively instead)
Step 4 of 6
⏱️ 3–5 minutes
3 Good Repetitions Are Worth More Than 10 Forced Ones.
Dosage Guidance
Target repetitions per session: 3–7 — not a fixed number, read the child. Vary texture, pressure, and temperature within sessions while maintaining the core principle.
Satiation Indicators — When Enough Is Enough
  • Body fully relaxed
  • Hands drop naturally to lap
  • Child shifts attention to something else
  • Child pushes material away gently
  • Yawning (sign of parasympathetic activation — success)
Variation Menu
Textured tool: Light strokes → firm pressure → rapid back-and-forth → circular. Build a "texture menu" across the session.
Fidget: Squeeze → pull → twist → roll → alternate hands. Time-based: "How long can we keep going?"
Deep pressure: Arms → shoulders → back → legs (child-led preference). Duration variation: 5-second squeezes → 20-second sustained pressure. Add movement: joint compressions during walking/bouncing.
What NOT To Do
  • Continue past satiation signals — this creates aversion
  • Introduce unfamiliar material without transition
  • Express disappointment if fewer repetitions than expected
Step 5 of 6
⏱️ 30 seconds–2 minutes
Timing Matters More Than Magnitude. Celebrate the Attempt, Not Just the Success.
Reinforcement Scripts — Exact Words
"You chose the [tool] instead! That's exactly right. Your hands are learning!"
"I noticed — you tried the [tool] when you felt that urge. I'm so proud."
"You touched it! That was brave. Let's do it again."

⏱️Timing Rule: Deliver reinforcement WITHIN 3 SECONDS of desired behavior. One clear, specific, genuine praise statement beats five generic "Good job!"s
Reinforcement Menu
Social
Warm hug, thumbs up, high five, 30-second cuddle
Tangible
Reward sticker, token added to reward jar — track every tool-use instead of scratching
Activity
Extra 5 minutes of preferred activity, choice of next activity
Natural
If using fidget during TV time — TV continues. The behavior itself was reinforced.
Every instance of tool-use instead of scratching = 1 token. X tokens = agreed preferred reward. This is ABA differential reinforcement executed at home.
Step 6 of 6
⏱️ 2–3 minutes
No Session Ends Abruptly. Every Session Lands Gently.
Transitions are when scratching is most likely to return. End the session in a way that maintains the regulated state. Always give a transition warning 2 minutes before ending.
Option A: Sensory Calm
Continue compression sleeve wearing. Child sits under weighted blanket. No demands, no expectations.
Option B: Proprioceptive
Firm sustained hug, "bear squeeze," or lying under pillow/cushion briefly.
Option C: Transition Object
Child holds a preferred comfort item as a bridge to the next activity.
Option D: Movement
Brief walk, jump on trampoline, or 5 deep breaths with parent.

If child resists ending: Do NOT increase demands. Give 1 more minute. "Just one more, then all done." Keep the promise. Use a visual timer — predictability reduces resistance.
60 Seconds of Data Now Saves Hours of Guessing Later.
Record just 3 data points after every session. Sustainability matters more than comprehensiveness — a simple habit you maintain beats a perfect system you abandon.
3 Essential Data Points
DATA POINT 1: Scratching frequency today □ None □ 1–3 times □ 4–10 times □ Constant
DATA POINT 2: Tool use today □ Used alternative spontaneously □ Used alternative with prompt □ Refused alternative □ Alternative not available
DATA POINT 3: Session outcome □ Full protocol completed □ Partial (steps: ___) □ Postponed (reason: ___)

Session Abandonment Is Not Failure. It's Data.
7 Common Problems — Exactly What To Do
Most techniques fail before the parent stops trying. Consistency through imperfect sessions is more valuable than perfect execution of occasional sessions.
Problem 1: Child refused all materials
Observe scratching closely — what does the motion look like? Fast/hard? Slow/rhythmic? Find a material that more closely mimics the exact motion and intensity. Try a completely different category (if textured tools failed, try cold; if cold failed, try deep pressure).
Problem 2: Child used tool once but returned to scratching
This is normal and expected. The alternative hasn't competed successfully yet — the habit loop is stronger than one exposure. Keep consistent, keep non-judgmental. 20–30 exposures before expecting habit-level redirection.
Problem 3: Works at home but not at school/community
Pack a portable sensory kit for every bag. Communicate with school about allowing sensory tools. Build consistency across settings. The regulated nervous system is context-specific until generalized.
Problem 4: Child scratches MORE when tools are out
Introduce tools proactively (BEFORE urges, as daily routine) rather than only when scratching occurs. Remove the crisis-response association entirely.
Problem 5: Child can't stop even with tools present
Switch to emotional regulation protocol. Bring compression and deep pressure. Consider functional assessment — is this anxiety-driven scratching requiring a different approach?
Problem 6: Scratching is worsening despite intervention
May indicate escalating anxiety, unmet need, or medical trigger (skin condition, allergy, infection-based itch). Consult Pinnacle OT. Medical review for skin/allergy. 📞 9100 181 181
Problem 7: Parent is too anxious to be calm during sessions
This is extremely common. Your nervous system matters too. Ask for parent support at your next Pinnacle consultation. Your regulated presence is the most powerful intervention you provide.
No Two Children Are Identical. Neither Should Their Intervention Be.
Difficulty Modifications
⬇️ Easier Modifications
Single material only (most familiar). 2-minute session. No expectations — just presence. More reinforcement density. Parent models without asking child to join. Compression sleeve as passive support all day.
⬆️ Harder Modifications
Introduce 2 materials in same session. Delay reinforcement slightly. Practice during mild stress to build generalization. Add awareness component. Begin using tools in community settings.
Sensory Profile Variations
🟠 Sensory Seeker
Primary: Textured tools (matched intensity) + Cold input. Avoid gentle/smooth fidgets — too low intensity.
🔵 Sensory Avoider
Primary: Emotional regulation tools + Compression. Avoid very intense textures that may cause additional distress.
⚪ Automatic/Habitual
Primary: Awareness tools + Fidgets for hand occupation. Avoid shame-based monitoring.
🟣 Mixed Function (Most Common)
Build a toolkit: one tool per function. Observe which context → which tool works.

Age-Based Modifications: Ages 2–4: Parent holds and guides. Very short sessions (2–3 min). Heavy play-based framing. | Ages 4–7: Child begins choosing preferred tool. Label-building begins. | Ages 7–10: Child participates in selecting toolkit. Awareness-based approaches more applicable. | Ages 10–12+: Child can self-report urges. Self-directed tool use. Identity-affirmative framing.
Progress Tracker
Weeks 1–2
Week 1–2: The Learning Phase. Expect Tolerance — Not Transformation.
Week 1–2 are the hardest weeks. The behavior may appear unchanged or even slightly more visible because you're watching more carefully. This is not the technique failing — it is the baseline being established. Your consistency in weeks 1–2 determines everything that follows.
✅ Observable Indicators for Weeks 1–2
Child is aware of the alternative material's existence · Child tolerates the material being present (even if not using it) · One or two successful redirections in the week (with heavy prompting) · Scratching frequency/intensity has not dramatically worsened
What "Progress" Actually Looks Like This Early
"If your child scratches AROUND the tool rather than AT it — that's the tool being considered. That's progress." "If your child held the fidget for 10 seconds before dropping it — that's 10 seconds of neural pathway building."
Progress Tracker
Weeks 3–4
Week 3–4: Neural Pathways Are Forming. Look for the Signs Most Parents Miss.
Consolidation Indicators
  • Child anticipates the tool — looks for it before scratching starts
  • Child picks up tool with prompt and uses it for 30+ seconds
  • Scratching intensity reducing even when frequency hasn't yet
  • Child touches wounds less frequently — healing is occurring
  • One or more unprompted reaching-for-tool moments observed
  • In some situations, child uses tool without scratching at all
Signs of Neural Pathway Formation
"The child starts to reach for the textured tool when they feel the urge — even before scratching begins. This is the competing response becoming automatic."
"You notice they fidget during TV without scratching — the fidget has entered the habit loop in place of scratching in this specific context."
"The child refers to their 'scratch tool' or 'safe scratch' — they're building language around the concept. This is generalization beginning."
When to Increase Frequency or Intensity
When you see 3+ consecutive days of consistent tool use: Add a second high-risk context · Introduce a second tool type · Begin light awareness work (if appropriate for age/profile)
Progress Tracker
Weeks 5–8
Week 5–8: Mastery Indicators. The Nervous System Has New Default Behaviors.
Primary Target Mastery
Child reaches for sensory tool in response to scratching urge in at least 3 out of 5 observed opportunities across 2+ different settings — without parent prompt.
Generalization Indicator
Tool use observed in at least 2 settings where training did not directly occur (e.g., trained at home, now using at school or in the car).
Skin Healing Indicator
Reduction in new wounds. Older wounds healing. Scabs not being reopened as frequently. Physical evidence of progress.
Mastery Badge Criteria
🏅 Spontaneous tool use in 3+ settings · 🏅 Unprompted verbal identification of urge: "I want to scratch" · 🏅 3+ days in a row with no new wounds · 🏅 Child demonstrates tool to another adult

When to Move to the Next Level: When current materials no longer provide adequate challenge/novelty · When generalization is occurring naturally · When emotional regulation component is ready to be deepened. → Next: D-406 Hair Pulling | D-430 Anxiety-Related Habits
You Did This. Your Child Grew Because of Your Commitment.
✨ What You've Built
A nervous system that has new options. A child who knows what to reach for when the urge comes. Skin that is healing and protected.
✨ Who You've Become
A parent who understands their child's sensory language. A family with a toolkit that works — because you made it work.
You started this page watching your child scratch until they bled, feeling helpless and afraid. You built a toolkit instead of fear. You showed up consistently when it was hard, when sessions didn't go perfectly, when you didn't see progress for 10 days straight. That consistency is why your child's nervous system is learning.
Mark this milestone. Tell your child, in whatever way they understand: "You've learned something new about yourself. You know how to help your nervous system. That's huge." Create a small ritual — a favorite meal, a special activity, a photograph. This moment matters.

📞9100 181 181 | Want to tell us about your win? We want to hear it.
Even in the Progress Zone — These Signs Mean Stop and Seek Support.
Trust your instincts. If something feels wrong, pause and ask. The escalation pathway below ensures every family gets the right level of support at the right time.
🚩 Flag 1: Scratching escalates significantly despite 4+ weeks of consistent intervention
New wounds every day, not reducing; child increasingly distressed. Do: Professional OT assessment → Functional behavior assessment → Medical review for underlying skin condition or allergy.
🚩 Flag 2: Repeated skin infections despite wound care
Wounds not healing, warmth/redness/discharge recurring. Do: Pediatrician/dermatologist immediately. Do not delay.
🚩 Flag 3: Scratching appears intentional self-harm
Child expresses self-hatred, wants to hurt self, severe shame response. Do: Mental health evaluation. This is beyond BFRB territory. 📞 9100 181 181 immediately.
🚩 Flag 4: New self-injurious behaviors emerging alongside scratching
Head-banging, biting self, hair-pulling beginning simultaneously. Do: Multi-behavior assessment. Contact Pinnacle for comprehensive functional analysis.
🚩 Flag 5: Scratching spreading to new body areas rapidly
Originally arms only → now face, scalp, neck. Do: Medical review + OT assessment + behavioral consultation concurrently.
🚩 Flag 6: Child experiencing significant psychological distress
Significant shame, social withdrawal due to skin appearance, depression indicators. Do: Child psychologist/mental health professional referral. Pinnacle can coordinate.

Questions Real Parents Ask. Answered by the Consortium.
Q: My child scratches at night while sleeping — do these materials work for sleep?
Yes, with specific modifications. Compression sleeves and thin cotton gloves during sleep reduce tissue damage even when scratching continues. Weighted blankets help regulate the nervous system during sleep, which may reduce nighttime scratching. A sensory diet with adequate proprioceptive input during the day also reduces nighttime urges. Address daytime scratching protocol first — nighttime usually follows.
Q: How long until we see real results?
Most families see initial redirection within 1–2 weeks. Meaningful reduction in scratching frequency: weeks 3–6. Consistent independent tool use: weeks 6–12. This timeline assumes daily consistency. Inconsistent implementation extends it. Severe BFRB with strong habit entrenchment may take longer and benefits from OT support.
Q: My child refuses all sensory tools. Everything gets thrown.
This is common early-stage behavior, not tool failure. Try: (1) Present tool to yourself first — child watches you use it. (2) Leave tool in child's environment without expectation — proximity builds familiarity. (3) Try a completely different material category. (4) Use during distraction (tool available while watching preferred content). (5) If refusal is universal → OT assessment for sensory defensiveness may be needed.
Q: Can my child use sensory tools at school?
Yes — this is a common accommodation for children with sensory needs. Subtle fidgets (small silicone rings, putty in a pocket) are appropriate during class. Speak to the school using the teacher template from Card 37. Under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act 2016 in India, reasonable accommodations are the child's right.
Q: Is self-scratching always BFRB or can it be medical?
Medical causes should be ruled out — especially for new-onset scratching. Skin conditions (eczema, dry skin), allergies, iron deficiency, and sensory sensitivities to fabrics or detergents can all drive scratching. If scratching emerged suddenly or correlates with specific skin areas or times, see a pediatrician/dermatologist before assuming behavioral function.
Q: What's the difference between BFRB scratching and self-harm?
BFRB scratching seeks sensation, regulation, or is automatic habit — not intentional injury. Signs suggesting intentional self-harm rather than BFRB: child expresses desire to hurt self, scratching used as self-punishment, strong shame response, occurs after conflicts. If you see these signs, mental health evaluation is essential. 📞 9100 181 181
Q: My child has autism and doesn't communicate. How do I know which function their scratching serves?
Systematic observation: Scratching during low-stimulation = likely sensory/boredom · During stressful transitions = likely anxiety · Without apparent environmental correlation = likely automatic/habit · In specific body areas with intensity variation = may be medical. An OT at Pinnacle can conduct formal functional observation assessment.
Q: Can I do too much sensory input? Can the sensory diet harm?
For most children, more appropriate sensory input is better than less. However: weighted items must be appropriate weight (10% body weight max). Deep pressure should be calming, not distressing. If a child becomes MORE dysregulated with a specific input, discontinue that input. An OT-designed sensory diet optimizes input type and quantity for the specific child's profile.
